note: Source says not to be in 'too great a hurry'; candidate drops 'too great'.
replacement: Alcibiades also advised Tissaphernes not to be in too great a hurry to end the war. He should refuse to be persuaded to bring up the Phoenician fleet that he was equipping, or to provide pay for more Hellenes, and so put the power by land and sea into the same hands. He should leave each of the contending parties in possession of one element, so that the king could call in the other whenever he found one troublesome. For if the command of the sea and land were united in one hand, the king would not know where to turn for help to overthrow the dominant power, unless he finally chose to stand up himself and go through with the struggle at great expense and hazard. The cheapest plan was to let the Hellenes wear each other out, at a small share of the expense and without risk to himself. Besides, he would find the Athenians the most convenient partners in empire, since they did not aim at conquests on land, and carried on the war on principles and in a manner most advantageous to the King. They were prepared to combine to conquer the sea for Athens, and for the King all the Hellenes inhabiting his country, whom the Peloponnesians, on the contrary, had come to liberate. Now it was not likely that the Lacedaemonians would free the Hellenes from the Hellenic Athenians without also freeing them from the barbarian Mede, unless he overthrew them first. Alcibiades therefore urged him to wear both sides out at first, and, after cutting down the Athenian power as far as he could, to rid the country of the Peloponnesians without delay. In the main Tissaphernes approved of this policy, so far at least as could be judged from his behavior. He now gave his confidence to Alcibiades in return for his good advice, and kept the Peloponnesians short of money. He would not let them fight at sea, and ruined their cause by pretending that the Phoenician fleet would arrive and that they would then be able to fight with the odds in their favor. In this way he made their navy, which had been very remarkable, lose its efficiency, and he showed a coolness toward the war that was too plain to be mistaken.

note: Source parenthesis around the aside on Alcibiades' message was removed.
replacement: Alcibiades gave this advice to Tissaphernes and the King, with whom he then was. He did so not merely because he thought it really the best, but because he was looking for means to bring about his restoration to his country. He knew well that if he did not destroy it, he might one day hope to persuade the Athenians to recall him, and he thought his best chance of persuading them lay in letting them see that he had the favor of Tissaphernes. The event proved him right. The Athenians at Samos learned that he had influence with Tissaphernes. They found this out mainly on their own initiative, (though partly also through Alcibiades himself, who sent word to their chief men to tell the best men in the army that he would be glad to return to his country and make Tissaphernes their friend, if only there were an oligarchy in place of the rascally democracy that had banished him). Upon this the captains and chief men in the armament at once embraced the idea of subverting the democracy.

note: Source parenthesis around the remark on Tissaphernes' fears was removed.
replacement: After this the Chians were besieged even more closely than before by land and sea, and the famine in the place was great. Meanwhile the Athenian envoys with Pisander arrived at the court of Tissaphernes and conferred with him about the proposed agreement. But Alcibiades was not altogether sure of Tissaphernes (who feared the Peloponnesians more than the Athenians and besides wished to wear out both parties, as Alcibiades himself had recommended). So he resorted to the following stratagem to make the treaty between the Athenians and Tissaphernes fail through the magnitude of his demands. In my opinion Tissaphernes wanted this result, his motive being fear. Alcibiades, for his part, now saw that Tissaphernes was determined not to treat on any terms, and he wished the Athenians to think, not that he was unable to persuade Tissaphernes, but that Tissaphernes had been persuaded and was willing to join them, and that they had not conceded enough to him. For the demands of Alcibiades, who spoke for Tissaphernes while he was present, were so extravagant that the Athenians had to bear the blame of the failure, although for a long while they agreed to whatever he asked. He required the cession of the whole of Ionia, then of the adjacent islands, besides other concessions, and these passed without opposition. At last, in the third interview, Alcibiades, who now feared that his inability would be completely discovered, required them to allow the King to build ships and sail along his own coast wherever he pleased and with as many ships as he pleased. At this the Athenians would yield no further. They concluded that nothing could be done and that they had been deceived by Alcibiades, and they went away in a passion and proceeded to Samos.

note: Two source parentheses (instructions to establish oligarchies; the banished party) were removed.
replacement: After encouraging each other in these resolutions, they at once sent off half the envoys together with Pisander to do what was necessary at Athens (with instructions to establish oligarchies on their way in all the subject cities they might touch at). The other half they dispatched in different directions to the other dependencies. Diitrephes also, who was in the neighborhood of Chios and had been elected to the command of the Thracian towns, was sent off to his government. Arriving at Thasos, he abolished the democracy there. Two months, however, had not passed after his departure before the Thasians began to fortify their town. They were already tired of an aristocracy under Athens and were expecting freedom from Lacedaemon every day. Indeed there was a party of them (whom the Athenians had banished) who were with the Peloponnesians. With their friends in the town they were already making every effort to bring a squadron and effect the revolt of Thasos. So this party saw exactly what it most wanted done, namely the reform of the government without risk and the abolition of the democracy that would have opposed it. Things at Thasos thus turned out just the opposite of what the oligarchical conspirators at Athens expected. The same, in my opinion, was the case in many of the other dependencies. The cities no sooner got a moderate government and liberty of action than they went on to absolute freedom, and were not at all seduced by the show of reform offered by the Athenians.
